title: Condensed matter
tagline: Why solids are metals, insulators or magnets
summary: Crystal lattices, phonons, the free-electron gas, band structure, semiconductors, and an introduction to magnetism and superconductivity.
overview: A solid is a quantum many-body problem with Avogadro’s number of particles. The reason it is solvable at all is symmetry: a crystal is periodic, so its excitations are waves labelled by a crystal momentum, and its electrons occupy bands rather than atomic orbitals. This course builds that picture from the lattice up.

Diffraction fixes the lattice. Lattice vibrations — phonons — are the normal modes of the coupled atoms and carry the heat capacity of an insulator. Electrons are treated first as a free Fermi gas, which already explains conduction and the heat capacity of a metal, and then as waves in a periodic potential, which opens gaps and distinguishes metals from insulators. Semiconductors are the technologically decisive case. Magnetism and superconductivity are introduced as broken symmetries, not as complete theories.

The reciprocal lattice and the first Brillouin zone do more work than any formula in the course. Draw them. A band structure is a plot of energy against crystal momentum in that zone, and almost every qualitative question about a solid is a question about that plot.
outcomes: Index crystal planes and use Bragg’s law to interpret a diffraction pattern.
Derive the phonon dispersion of a monatomic and a diatomic chain, and the Debye heat capacity.
Apply the free-electron model: Fermi energy, density of states, and the electronic heat capacity.
Explain band gaps with the nearly-free-electron model and state Bloch’s theorem.
Describe electrons and holes in a semiconductor and the p–n junction in outline.
Distinguish diamagnetism, paramagnetism and ferromagnetism, and state the phenomenological facts of superconductivity.

history.title: Diffraction by a crystal
history.detail: Max von Laue proposed that a crystal would diffract X-rays. Friedrich and Knipping observed the spots the same year, and the Braggs turned the observation into a law and a method in 1913.

history.title: Drude’s metal
history.detail: Paul Drude treated conduction electrons as a classical gas. Sommerfeld replaced the classical distribution by a Fermi gas in 1927, which is the free-electron model of this course.

history.title: Bloch’s theorem
history.detail: Felix Bloch proved that the eigenstates of an electron in a periodic potential are plane waves modulated by a periodic function, the starting point of band theory.

history.title: Superconductivity
history.detail: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes found that the resistance of mercury vanishes below 4.2 K. The microscopic theory, by Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, came in 1957.

history.title: The transistor
history.detail: Bardeen and Brattain demonstrated the point-contact transistor in December 1947; Shockley’s junction transistor followed. The device is a p–n junction put to work.

history.title: The quantum Hall effect
history.detail: Klaus von Klitzing found that the Hall conductance of a two-dimensional electron gas is quantised in units of e²/h. It is the cleanest macroscopic quantum effect in a solid.
